taxonomy.subtopic: Diastolic backflow, wide pulse pressure, and loss of isovolumetric phases

questions.stem_html:
A 48-year-old man with infective endocarditis develops a new high-pitched early diastolic murmur along the left sternal border. His pulse is bounding, and blood pressure is 158/48 mm Hg. Echocardiography shows severe aortic regurgitation and acute left ventricular volume overload. A pressure-volume loop is constructed.

Which change is most characteristic of the loop in this patient?

options.text_html: A lower end-diastolic volume with preservation of both isovolumetric phases
A markedly increased end-systolic pressure caused by fixed outflow obstruction
Complete elimination of ventricular ejection into the aorta
A narrow pulse pressure from reduced diastolic runoff
Loss of true isovolumetric relaxation and contraction because ventricular volume changes while the aortic valve is incompetent

questions.explanation_html: During diastole, blood enters the ventricle from both the left atrium and aorta. During the nominal isovolumetric contraction interval, regurgitant flow can persist until aortic pressure is exceeded. Thus ventricular volume changes during both phases that normally have closed valves. An incompetent aortic valve prevents the left ventricle from having a truly closed chamber during the usual isovolumetric intervals.

wrong_choice_explanations.1: Aortic regurgitation increases ventricular filling and abolishes the closed-valve intervals.
wrong_choice_explanations.2: Fixed high systolic pressure is characteristic of aortic stenosis, not regurgitant diastolic flow.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: Forward ejection persists, although part of the stroke volume returns during diastole.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Aortic regurgitation causes increased systolic stroke volume and rapid diastolic runoff, widening pulse pressure.

questions.educational_objective: Relate aortic regurgitation to wide pulse pressure, increased left ventricular end-diastolic volume, and loss of normal isovolumetric phases on the pressure-volume loop.
